Q: "Connection refused" while trying to connect to docker mysql container A:

I assume you are trying to connect from another container/service defined in docker-compose and you are using current version of docker-compose (2.4 or 3.7)

You need to change

DATABASE_URL=mysql://root:symf0ny@127.0.0.1:3306/iym

to

DATABASE_URL=mysql://root:symf0ny@mysql:3306/iym

The reason is that 127.0.0.1 is refering to the localhost of the machine on which php runs. In this case it's the php's container localhost. But the db doesn't run there. It runs in another docker container, which can be reached under the service name, mysql in this case.

See docker-compose networking docs

By default Compose sets up a single network for your app. Each container for a service joins the default network and is both reachable by other containers on that network, and discoverable by them at a hostname identical to the container name.

The service is not only discoverable under the container name (which is automatically generated to projectName_serviceName_1, project name begin by default folder name), but also under service name, link and service alias if defined. I would recommend using service name wherever possible.

More in docs: https://docs.docker.com/compose/networking/

Q: Is the brute-force "Balanced Binary Tree" solution really O(n^2) with early exit? A:

The catch you are falling into, is considering that detecting the height of balanced binary tree, with n nodes, takes O(log n) time, because you implicitly assume that you only follow the path from the subtree root, to the leaves. The truth is that this exhaustive algorithm, retroactively traverses all nodes of a certain subtree, in order to find the subtree height.

It's kind of tricky to show a figure in SO, but you can perhaps try Wikipedia. In short, in order to find the height of the root, you have to traverse subtrees having at most, n/2 nodes each. Their height is respectively computed by traversing subtrees of n/4 nodes each, and so on.

This will give a formula of 2*n/2 + 4*n/4 + ... + n*1, which is a progression giving O(n2). The last term (n*1) is the trivial cost of finding the height of the, n in number (or in fact n/2 if I am not wrong), leave nodes, an operation costing O(1)

Q: Data manipulation/time calculation in R with lubridate A:

You can treat short events (<5 seconds) as noise, remove them, and then recalculate durations by collapsing consecutive events. The key idea is to recompute durations after filtering, not before.

A tidy way to do this is:

  1. Order events by individual, nest, and time

  2. Compute durations between consecutive enter/exit events

  3. Remove events with duration < 5 seconds

  4. Recalculate durations again on the cleaned sequence

Example logic using dplyr:

library(dplyr)

cleaned <- df %>%
  arrange(individual_id, nest_id, time) %>%
  group_by(individual_id, nest_id) %>%
  mutate(
    duration = difftime(lead(time), time, units = "secs")
  ) %>%
  filter(is.na(duration) | duration >= 5) %>%
  mutate(
    duration = difftime(lead(time), time, units = "secs")
  )

This effectively ignores mistaken entrances and recalculates time spent in or out of the nest as if they never happened.
